questions.problem: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(5,10)$ and $Y∼N(6,11).$ Find the distribution of the random variable $W=2X-5Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2})$, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}W=2X-5Y & ∼N(2\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 6,{2}^{2}\cdot 10+(-5)^{2}\cdot 11) \\  & ∼N(-20,315).\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore, $W∼N(-20,315).$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=4{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2} & ∼N(4{\mu }_{1}-2{\mu }_{2},16{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+4{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20-16,48+16) \\  & ∼N(4,64).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =4$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{64}=8.$ 

We want to find $P(Y<14).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<14) & =P(Z<\frac{14-4}{8}) \\  & =P(Z<1.25) \\  & =Φ(1.25)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.25)≈0.8944.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y<14)≈0.89.
$$

questions.problem:
The weights of some chocolate cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $10\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $1\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weights of some oatcakes are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $2\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$  If one chocolate cookie and one oatcake are randomly selected, what is the probability that $6$ times the weight of the cookie plus $4$ times the weight of oatcake is less than $120\,\text{g}$, but more than $100\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights of the cookies and oatcakes are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-2.5\,$ | $\,0.0062\,$ | $\,0.0060\,$ | $\,0.0059\,$ | $\,0.0057\,$ | $\,0.0055\,$ |
| $\,-2.4\,$ | $\,0.0082\,$ | $\,0.0080\,$ | $\,0.0078\,$ | $\,0.0075\,$ | $\,0.0073\,$ |
| $\,-2.3\,$ | $\,0.0107\,$ | $\,0.0104\,$ | $\,0.0102\,$ | $\,0.0099\,$ | $\,0.0096\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the weight of a chocolate cookie, and let $Y$ denote the weight of an oatcake. We want to find 

$$
P(100<6X+4Y<120).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(10,1)$ and $Y∼N(15,2),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}6X+4Y & ∼N(6\cdot 10+4\cdot 15,36\cdot 1+16\cdot 2) \\  & ∼N(120,68).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $6X+4Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =120$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{68}.$

To find $P(100<6X+4Y<120),$ we convert $6X+4Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<6X+4Y<120) & =P(\frac{100-120}{\sqrt{68}}<Z<\frac{120-120}{\sqrt{68}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.43<Z<0) \\  & =P(Z<0)-P(Z\le -2.43) \\  & =P(Z\le 0)-P(Z\le -2.43) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-2.43)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.43) & ≈0.0075,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<6X+4Y<120) & ≈Φ(0)-Φ(-2.43) \\  & =0.5-0.0075 \\  & ≈0.4925.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A factory produces shovels, each consisting of a handle and a blade.
The length of a handle is normally distributed with a mean of $120$ centimeters and a variance of $0.14,$  while the length of a blade is normally distributed with a mean of $30$ centimeters and a variance of $0.02.$ If one shovel is randomly selected, what is the probability that its length is more than $150$ centimeters, but less than $150.5$ centimeters? You may assume that the lengths are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ | $\,0.8962\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |
| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9115\,$ | $\,0.9131\,$ | $\,0.9147\,$ | $\,0.9162\,$ | $\,0.9177\,$ |
| $\,1.4\,$ | $\,0.9265\,$ | $\,0.9279\,$ | $\,0.9292\,$ | $\,0.9306\,$ | $\,0.9319\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the length of a handle, and let $Y$ denote the length of a blade. We want to find 

$$
P(150<X+Y<150.5).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(120,0.14)$ and $Y∼N(30,0.02)$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(120+30,0.14+0.02) \\  & ∼N(150,0.16).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =150$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.16}=0.4.$

In order to find $P(150<X+Y<150.5),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(150<X+Y<150.5) & =P(\frac{150-150}{0.4}<Z<\frac{150.5-150}{0.4}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.25) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.25)-P(Z\le 0) \\  & =Φ(1.25)-Φ(0)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & ≈0.8944,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(150<X+Y<150.5) & ≈Φ(1.25)-Φ(0) \\  & ≈0.8944-0.5 \\  & ≈0.3944.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the length of a randomly selected shovel is more than $150$ centimeters, but less than $150.5$ centimeters is $0.3944.$

questions.problem: If ${X}_{1}∼N(-3,1)$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(1,2)$ are independent, then what is the distribution of $Y={X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+3{X}_{2} & ∼N(1\cdot (-3)+3\cdot 1,{1}^{2}\cdot 1+{3}^{2}\cdot 2) \\  & ∼N(0,19).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y∼N(0,19).$
